title: Solving Agentic AI Fleet Challenges with NVIDIA Vera CPU | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA uses telemetry from 163,594 agentic sessions — over 97% with unique trajectory profiles — to argue that agentic CPU fleets should optimize completed user sessions rather than core count, and claims the Vera CPU with Olympus cores delivers up to 1.5x the per-core agentic performance of AMD's Venice on internally measured, estimated SPEC CPU 2026 results. The competitive attack is explicitly aimed at high-core-count, chiplet-based server CPUs that trade single-thread latency for density.

insights.claim: Telemetry from 163,594 agentic sessions shows over 97% had unique trajectory profiles, which NVIDIA uses to argue that right-sizing a datacenter CPU fleet around multiple specialized design points is impractical for agentic workloads.
insights.speaker: Eduardo Alvarez
insights.so_what: If workload variance really defeats specialization, the server CPU market for AI factories consolidates toward one balanced SKU — favoring whoever owns the platform bundle rather than the widest SKU ladder.
insights.quote: Based on telemetry from 163,594 agentic sessions, over 97% of sessions showed unique trajectory profiles (Figure 1).
insights.locator: AI factories are interconnected systems where fleet economics

insights.claim: An agentic trajectory can be characterized by two dimensions — length (reasoning steps, tool calls, retries, sub-tasks before a turn resolves) and width (concurrent tool calls, retrieval operations, sandboxes, sub-agents at each stage).
insights.speaker: Eduardo Alvarez
insights.so_what: A clean two-axis model for sizing any agent-serving infrastructure: width sets concurrency requirements, length sets single-thread latency requirements.
insights.locator: The shape of an agentic trajectory is defined by its length and width

insights.claim: Production telemetry shows agentic execution is a long sequential reasoning chain punctuated by sporadic parallel bursts, and the sequential path is strictly latency-bound — the main agent idles waiting on fan-out completion, so per-thread speed governs end-to-end session time even in wide sessions.
insights.speaker: Eduardo Alvarez
insights.so_what: Single-thread performance, a metric the market had written off for datacenter CPUs, becomes the binding constraint on agent throughput — a re-rating vector for latency-optimized cores.
insights.quote: the dominant sequential path is strictly latency-bound—governing overall session completion time
insights.locator: Production telemetry also reveals how these diverse trajectories unfold

insights.claim: NVIDIA cites a real Claude Code session as its exemplar workload, where the main agent advanced through a long sequential trajectory for most of a 33-minute run with brief sub-agent fan-out bursts.
insights.speaker: Eduardo Alvarez
insights.so_what: Coding agents have become the reference workload silicon vendors design against — a signal on which agentic use case is currently driving the most infrastructure spend.
insights.quote: In the real-world Claude Code session shown in Figure 3, the main agent advances through a long sequential trajectory for most of the 33-minute run.
insights.locator: What real agent sessions look like

insights.claim: The correct optimization target for an agentic CPU fleet is total completed user sessions, not raw core count — an explicit attempt to change the metric server CPUs are benchmarked and purchased on.
insights.speaker: Eduardo Alvarez
insights.so_what: Watch whether hyperscaler procurement adopts sessions-per-rack as a spec; a metric change is how an entrant reframes a market it does not yet lead on core count.
insights.quote: the relevant optimization target for an agentic CPU fleet is the total number of completed user sessions, not raw core count
insights.locator: This is why the relevant optimization target

insights.claim: High-core-count CPUs are framed as looking efficient on paper while forcing a trade-off — sacrificing the single-thread performance needed on the agent's critical path in order to hit core density targets.
insights.speaker: Eduardo Alvarez
insights.so_what: A direct attack on the core-count arms race that has driven AMD's server share gains; the counter-argument to test is whether agentic fan-out width grows fast enough to restore density's advantage.
insights.quote: High-core-count systems might appear efficient on paper, but they often force a trade-off.
insights.locator: This is why the relevant optimization target

insights.claim: Disabling cores to boost single-thread performance strands the memory attached to them — leaving 8 GB per core unused and up to 1.5 TB of memory capacity stranded, imposing a significant memory TCO penalty.
insights.speaker: Eduardo Alvarez
insights.so_what: Ties CPU architecture directly to DRAM spend: with memory prices elevated, stranded capacity per socket is a real line item in AI factory TCO models.
insights.quote: This can leave 8 GB per core unused and impose a significant memory TCO penalty (Figure 4).
insights.locator: At any given moment, a CPU can effectively “turn off” cores

insights.claim: A single balanced CPU design point removes the need to fragment an AI factory fleet across multiple specialized SKUs, which NVIDIA presents as the operational and procurement advantage of Vera over a mixed fleet.
insights.speaker: Eduardo Alvarez
insights.so_what: Fleet homogeneity is a procurement lock-in argument as much as a technical one — it favors single-vendor platform bundles over best-of-breed sourcing.
insights.locator: An optimal agentic fleet just needs a single CPU design point

insights.claim: Vera's NVIDIA Olympus cores are designed to sustain per-thread performance while the full socket is active, using a wide front end, advanced branch prediction, deep out-of-order execution and a high-bandwidth memory subsystem to handle branch-heavy, dependency-heavy agent code.
insights.speaker: Eduardo Alvarez
insights.so_what: Loaded per-core performance, not peak boost on one core, is the spec to demand — vendors quoting single-core turbo numbers are answering a different question.
insights.locator: How Vera CPUs deliver this balance

insights.claim: NVIDIA attributes part of Vera's advantage to a low-latency monolithic die rather than a chiplet topology, claiming it reduces topology-driven stalls and performance variability across agentic execution phases.
insights.speaker: Eduardo Alvarez
insights.so_what: A monolithic-versus-chiplet argument aimed squarely at AMD's packaging strategy; it also implies yield and die-size cost exposure for NVIDIA that chiplet designs avoid.
insights.quote: Vera CPU’s low-latency monolithic architecture further reduces topology-driven stalls and variability across these phases.
insights.locator: An optimal agentic fleet just needs a single CPU design point

insights.claim: NVIDIA claims Vera delivers up to 1.5x the per-core agentic performance of AMD Venice across four agentic workloads including compiler, static analysis and Python benchmarks, based on estimated SPEC CPU 2026 results.
insights.speaker: Eduardo Alvarez
insights.so_what: The first head-to-head Vera-versus-Venice number in the market; it sets the anchor competitors must rebut and frames NVIDIA as a direct threat to AMD's datacenter CPU franchise.
insights.quote: NVIDIA Vera CPU delivers up to 1.5x the agentic performance of the latest competition.
insights.locator: The estimated SPEC CPU® 2026 results in Figure 5

insights.claim: The comparison rests on NVIDIA's own July 2026 internal measurements, with AMD Venice per-workload performance estimated from a SPECrate 2026_int_base score of 2070 and normalized using internal Turin measurements — not a like-for-like independent benchmark.
insights.speaker: Eduardo Alvarez
insights.so_what: Discount the 1.5x headline until third-party SPEC submissions land; estimated-and-normalized competitor scores are the standard tell for a favorable configuration.
insights.quote: Individual workload performance for Venice was estimated based on SPECrate®2026_int_base score 2070 with components normalized based on internal Turin measurements.
insights.locator: NVIDIA Vera SPEC CPU® 2026 results measured internally in July 2026
